explicacao: O tear de Jacquard era controlado por uma corrente de cartões perfurados. Cada cartão correspondia a uma fileira do desenho: onde havia furo, uma haste passava e um mecanismo levantava o fio correspondente; onde havia papelão, o fio ficava no lugar. Trocar os cartões mudava o padrão, e quanto mais cartões, mais sofisticado o desenho. Como podia ser operado por uma só pessoa, o tear fazia tecidos decorados mais de 20 vezes mais rápido que os teares tradicionais. O retrato, feito pela casa Didier Petit, era tão detalhado que, segundo Babbage, dois membros da Royal Academy o tomaram por uma gravura. Ele recebia a elite britânica em casa e conta que, diante do quadro, o duque de Wellington perguntou se era uma gravura, e o príncipe Albert, que já conhecia o segredo, respondeu que não. Para Babbage, o fascínio estava no mecanismo: os cartões de Jacquard inspiraram a máquina analítica, que ele projetou para receber números e instruções da mesma forma. Ada Lovelace resumiu a ideia ao dizer que a máquina "tece padrões algébricos" assim como o tear de Jacquard tece flores e folhas.

fontes.titulo: The French Connection (Science History Institute, Distillations)
fontes.trecho: An 1839 woven silk portrait of French textile merchant and inventor Joseph-Marie Jacquard, recently added to CHF’s collections. [...] Babbage wanted a copy to show off in his London home, where he often entertained members of the British elite. Three years later he welcomed a pair of very special guests, the Duke of Wellington and Queen Victoria’s husband, Prince Albert. [...] When we had arrived in front of the portrait, I pointed it out as the object to which I solicited the Prince’s attention. “Oh! that engraving?” remarked the Duke of Wellington. “No!” said Prince Albert to the Duke; “it is not an engraving.” The prince had seen another copy of Jacquard’s portrait, based on a painting by Claude Bonnefond, and knew its secret. As Babbage explained later, it was a “sheet of woven silk, framed and glazed, but looking so perfectly like an engraving, that it had been mistaken for such by two members of the Royal Academy.” For Babbage the portrait was much more than a fine example of textile arts: what fascinated him was the mechanism through which it was created. [...] Each card passed before an array of circular metal rods corresponding to different warp threads. Whenever a rod came into contact with solid cardboard, its associated warp thread stayed in place. If it passed through a hole, then a mechanism lifted the thread. [...] Since his new loom could be overseen by a single person, decorated fabrics could be produced more than 20 times faster than with traditional looms. Unlike drum-based systems, which were best suited for repeating patterns, there were no limits to the possible outputs of a Jacquard loom—the greater the number of cards, the greater the sophistication of the design. Didier Petit and Company used approximately 24,000 cards to produce the Jacquard portrait that had caught Babbage’s eye. [...] he set it aside to pursue a more ambitious project directly inspired by Jacquard’s handiwork. [...] Lovelace recognized that what distinguished the analytical engine from other calculating machines was the use of punch cards to supply numeric inputs and instructions [...] “We may say most aptly that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves.”

The machine was controlled by a "chain of cards"; a number of punched cards laced together into a continuous sequence. Multiple rows of holes were punched on each card, with one complete card corresponding to one row of the design. [...] This use of replaceable punched cards to control a sequence of operations is considered an important step in the history of computing hardware, having inspired Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.

gancho: Quando despertadores não eram baratos nem confiáveis, trabalhadores ingleses pagavam alguns centavos por semana a um "despertador humano", que batia na janela com uma vara comprida ou até atirava ervilhas secas.
explicacao: O ofício, chamado em inglês de knocker-up, surgiu durante a Revolução Industrial na Grã-Bretanha, na Holanda, na Irlanda e em outros países, e era comum em cidades industriais grandes, como Manchester. Para as portas, usava-se um bastão curto e pesado; para as janelas dos andares de cima, uma vara longa e leve, muitas vezes de bambu. Alguns só iam embora quando tinham certeza de que o cliente acordara; outros davam umas batidas e seguiam. O serviço costumava ficar com homens idosos e mulheres grávidas, e às vezes policiais o faziam nas rondas da madrugada para reforçar o salário. E quem acordava o despertador? Muitos eram notívagos, que dormiam de dia e levantavam por volta das 4 da tarde. Em Ferryhill, cidade mineira do condado de Durham, as casas tinham lousas na parede externa, onde os mineiros escreviam a giz o horário do turno. Uma foto de 1931 mostra Mary Smith, no leste de Londres, com um tubo para soprar ervilhas, e a filha dela, Molly Moore, dizia ter sido a última a exercer a profissão. Nos anos 1940 e 1950, o ofício praticamente desapareceu, mas resistiu em alguns cantos industriais da Inglaterra até o começo dos anos 1970.

fontes.trecho: A knocker-up or knocker-upper had the job of rousing sleeping people so they could get to work on time. The role started during the Industrial Revolution, in Britain, the Netherlands, Ireland and some other countries, when alarm clocks were neither cheap nor reliable. By the 1940s and 1950s, the job had more or less entirely died out, although it still continued in some pockets of industrial England until the early 1970s. The knocker-up used a baton or short, heavy stick to knock on the clients' doors or a long and light stick, often made of bamboo, to reach windows on higher floors. One famous photograph shot in 1931 by John Topham shows Mary Smith in East London using a pea-shooter. In return for the task, the knocker-up would be paid a few pence a week. Some knocker-ups would not leave a client's window until they were sure that the client had been awakened, while others simply tapped several times and then moved on. Many knocker-uppers were night owls who slept during the day and woke around 4pm, thus not requiring a knocker-upper themselves. [...] There were large numbers of people carrying out the job, especially in larger industrial towns such as Manchester. Generally the job was done by elderly men and pregnant women but sometimes police constables supplemented their pay by performing the task during early morning patrols. Molly Moore (daughter of Mary Smith, also a knocker-up [...] claims to have been the last knocker-up to have been employed as such. Both Smith and Moore used a long rubber tube to shoot dried peas at their clients' windows. In Ferryhill, County Durham, miners' houses had slate boards set into their outside walls onto which the miners would write their shift details in chalk

gancho: Em 1865, um economista inglês argumentou que máquinas a vapor mais eficientes não tinham feito o país gastar menos carvão, e sim muito mais. O efeito, chamado paradoxo de Jevons, ainda divide economistas.
explicacao: William Stanley Jevons expôs a ideia no livro The Coal Question. Na época, muitos britânicos temiam que as reservas de carvão estivessem acabando depressa, e alguns especialistas confiavam que a tecnologia reduziria o consumo. Jevons disse que não. A máquina de James Watt era muito mais eficiente que a de Thomas Newcomen, e isso tornou o carvão uma fonte de força mais vantajosa. O vapor se espalhou por um grande número de indústrias, e o consumo total disparou, embora cada aplicação pedisse menos carvão. Para ele, era confusão de ideias achar que usar o combustível com economia fosse o mesmo que consumir menos. O mecanismo está no preço: quando a eficiência barateia o uso de um recurso e a demanda reage com força, o uso a mais pode superar a economia. Hoje isso é estudado como "efeito rebote", e há bastante debate sobre o tamanho dele e sobre o peso do paradoxo nas políticas de conservação de energia. Nem sempre ele acontece: os grandes ganhos de produtividade na agricultura baixaram o preço da comida sem fazer a demanda por alimentos crescer na mesma medida.

fontes.trecho: The Jevons paradox (pronounced , JEV-ənz) or Jevons effect is an economic phenomenon said to occur when technological improvements that increase the efficiency of a resource's use lead to a rise, rather than a fall, in total consumption of that resource. Greater efficiency reduces the amount of the resource needed per application, lowering its effective cost; if demand is sufficiently price elastic, this induces demand, frequently resulting in a net increase of total resource consumption. [...] Considerable debate exists about the size of the rebound in energy efficiency and the relevance of the Jevons paradox to energy conservation. [...] The Jevons paradox was first described by the English economist William Stanley Jevons in his 1865 book The Coal Question. Jevons observed that England's consumption of coal soared after James Watt introduced the Watt steam engine, which greatly improved the efficiency of the coal-fired steam engine from Thomas Newcomen's earlier design. Watt's innovations made coal a more cost-effective power source, leading to the increased use of the steam engine in a wide range of industries. This in turn increased total coal consumption, even as the amount of coal required for any particular application fell. Jevons argued that improvements in fuel efficiency tend to increase (rather than decrease) fuel use, writing: "It is a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth." At that time, many in Britain worried that coal reserves were rapidly dwindling, but some experts opined that improving technology would reduce coal consumption. [...] This increase in demand is known as the rebound effect [...] As an example of where the paradox did not occur, large improvements in farming productivity (including the Third Agricultural Revolution) led to lower food prices but did not result in increased demand for food

gancho: Em 1829, uma ferrovia inglesa fez um concurso para decidir se usaria locomotivas. Uma das concorrentes era movida por um cavalo andando numa esteira, e saiu da disputa quando o animal atravessou o piso.
explicacao: A Liverpool and Manchester Railway estava quase pronta, e os diretores ainda pensavam em puxar os trens com cabos acionados por máquinas a vapor fixas. O engenheiro da linha, George Stephenson, defendia as locomotivas. Para tirar a dúvida, a companhia organizou as provas de Rainhill, em outubro de 1829, com prêmio de 500 libras. Dez máquinas foram inscritas, mas só cinco estavam prontas no primeiro dia. A Cycloped, de Thomas Shaw Brandreth, foi a primeira a sair, depois do acidente com o cavalo. A Perseverance chegou danificada pelo transporte, passou cinco dias em conserto e não atingiu as 10 milhas por hora exigidas; ganhou um prêmio de consolação de 25 libras. A Novelty, favorita do público, chegou a 28 milhas por hora no primeiro dia, mas teve um cano da caldeira danificado. A Sans Pareil rachou um cilindro. Só a Rocket completou as provas, e os Stephenson ganharam o contrato para fornecer as locomotivas da linha. Em 2002, réplicas refizeram a disputa, e as contas indicaram que a Rocket ainda venceria, por ser bem mais confiável.

fontes.trecho: The Rainhill trials were a competition run from 6 to 14 October 1829 to test George Stephenson's argument that locomotives would have the best motive power for the nearly-completed Liverpool and Manchester Railway (L&MR). Ten locomotives were entered, of which five were able to compete [...] The directors of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway had originally intended to use stationary steam engines to haul trains along the railway using cables. They had appointed George Stephenson as their engineer of the line in 1826, and he strongly advocated for the use of steam locomotives instead. [...] A prize of £500 (equal to £47,460 today) was offered to the winner of the trials. [...] Cycloped, a horse-powered locomotive built by Thomas Shaw Brandreth. [...] Cycloped was the first to drop out of the competition. It used a horse walking on a drive belt for power and was withdrawn after an accident caused the horse to burst through the floor of the engine. The next locomotive to retire was Perseverance, which was damaged in transit to the competition. Burstall spent the first five days of the trials repairing his locomotive, and though it ran on the sixth day, it failed to reach the required 10 miles per hour (16 km/h) speed and was withdrawn from the trial. It was granted a £25 consolation prize [...] It completed eight trips before cracking a cylinder. [...] It was the crowd favourite and reached a then-astonishing 28 miles per hour (45 km/h) on the first day of competition. It later suffered damage to a boiler pipe which could not be fixed properly on site. [...] The Rocket was the only locomotive that completed the trials. [...] The Stephensons were given the contract to produce locomotives for the L&MR. [...] In a 2002 restaging of the Rainhill trials using replica engines [...] it was found that Rocket would still have won, as its relatively modern technology made it a much more reliable locomotive than the others.

gancho: A primeira grande ponte de ferro fundido do mundo, aberta em 1781 na Inglaterra, foi projetada como se fosse de madeira: suas peças se prendem com encaixes de carpinteiro, como espiga e cauda de andorinha.
explicacao: A Iron Bridge cruza um desfiladeiro do rio Severn, em Shropshire, perto de Coalbrookdale, onde Abraham Darby I começara a fundir minério de ferro com coque em 1709. O projeto segue um desenho que os carpinteiros usavam em estruturas de madeira. Thomas Gregory, encarregado da fundição que desenhou as peças em detalhe, adotou juntas típicas de marcenaria, como a de espiga e encaixe e a de cauda de andorinha. A obra consumiu cerca de 384,6 toneladas de ferro, divididas em quase 1.700 componentes, e o arco tem 30,63 metros de vão. Nada era padronizado: cada peça foi fundida para encaixar nas vizinhas, e peças "idênticas" em pontos diferentes chegam a diferir em vários centímetros. A ponte passou numa prova dura em 1795, quando uma grande cheia do Severn levou todas as pontes da região, menos ela, cuja estrutura vazada deixou a água passar. O sucesso inspirou o uso do ferro fundido em muitas pontes seguintes. E a cor dela mudou: numa restauração concluída em 2018, análises indicaram que o tom original era um marrom-avermelhado, e a ponte trocou o cinza-azulado por ele.

fontes.trecho: The Iron Bridge is a cast iron arch bridge that spans the Ironbridge Gorge of the River Severn in Shropshire, England. Opened in 1781, it was the first major bridge in the world to be made of cast iron. Its success inspired the widespread use of cast iron as a structural material [...] Abraham Darby I first smelted local iron ore with coke made from Coalbrookdale coal in 1709 [...] The bridge is to a carpenters' design typically used for wood structures, built from five sectional cast-iron ribs that give a span of 100 feet 6 inches (30.63 m). [...] Exactly 378 long tons 10 cwt (847,800 lb or 384.6 t) of iron was used in the construction of the bridge, and there are almost 1,700 individual components [...] Components were cast individually to fit with each other, rather than being of standard sizes, with discrepancies of up to several centimetres between 'identical' components in different locations. [...] A foreman at the foundry, Thomas Gregory, drew the detailed designs for the members, resulting in the use of carpentry jointing details such as mortise and tenon joints and dovetails. [...] In 1795, a large flood in the Severn swept away all the bridges in the vicinity, except the Iron Bridge, where the open structure allowed the floodwaters to pass through. [...] Following the works the bridge was reopened on 6 December 2018. [...] the bridge was also reverted from blue-grey to its original red-brown colour after forensic analysis revealed this was how the bridge looked when it was first erected.

gancho: Conta-se que a máquina de fiar "spinning jenny" tem o nome de uma filha do inventor, que teria derrubado uma roca. Mas os registros da igreja mostram que ele não tinha filha nem esposa chamada Jenny.
explicacao: James Hargreaves inventou a máquina por volta de 1764–1765, em Lancashire. Ela fiava vários fios ao mesmo tempo: no começo, oito fusos girados por uma única roda, número que mais tarde chegou a 120. Segundo a história mais contada, a filha ou a esposa dele, Jenny, derrubou uma roca, que continuou girando com o fuso em pé, e Hargreaves percebeu que nada obrigava os fusos a ficarem deitados. Os registros paroquiais de Church Kirk mostram que ele teve várias filhas, nenhuma chamada Jenny, e a esposa também não tinha esse nome. Uma explicação mais provável é que "jenny" fosse uma abreviação de "engine", máquina. A lenda circula até com o nome da esposa de Thomas Highs, que também se dizia o inventor. A história verdadeira teve outro tipo de drama: com a máquina, o preço do fio caiu, e os fiandeiros de Blackburn, revoltados, invadiram a casa de Hargreaves e quebraram as máquinas. Ele fugiu para Nottingham em 1768, passou a fabricá-las em segredo e as patenteou em 1770. Quando tentou processar quem usava cópias, o caso desmoronou ao se descobrir que ele próprio já tinha vendido várias.

fontes.trecho: It was invented in 1764–1765 by James Hargreaves in Stanhill, Oswaldtwistle, Lancashire in England. The device reduced the amount of work needed to produce cloth, with a worker able to work eight or more spools at once. This grew to 120 as technology advanced. [...] The idea was developed by Hargreaves as a metal frame with eight wooden spindles at one end. [...] The spinner used their right hand to rapidly turn a wheel which caused all the spindles to revolve, and the thread to be spun. [...] The price of yarn fell, angering the large spinning community in Blackburn. Eventually they broke into his house and smashed his machines, forcing him to flee to Nottingham in 1768. [...] There he set up shop producing jennies in secret for one Mr Shipley [...] On 12 July 1770, he took out a patent (no. 962) on his invention [...] but the case eventually fell apart when it was learned he had sold several in the past. [...] The most common story told about the invention of the device and the origin of the jenny in the machine's name is that one of his daughters (or his wife) named Jenny knocked over one of their own spinning wheels. The device kept working normally, with the spindle now pointed upright. Hargreaves realised there was no particular reason the spindles had to be horizontal, as they always had been, and he could place them vertically in a row. [...] The Registers of Church Kirk show that Hargreaves had several daughters, but none named Jenny (neither was his wife). A more likely explanation of the name is that jenny was an abbreviation of engine. Thomas Highs of Leigh has claimed to be the inventor and the story is repeated using his wife's name.

gancho: A lei britânica proibia exportar os projetos das máquinas têxteis. Em 1789, um jovem de 21 anos decorou o que pôde, foi para os EUA, onde as reconstruiu com o que guardou na cabeça. Em casa, virou "Slater, o Traidor".
explicacao: Samuel Slater começou a trabalhar aos dez anos na fiação de algodão de Jedediah Strutt, em Belper, que usava a water frame, a máquina de fiar movida a água de Richard Arkwright. Depois, como aprendiz de Strutt, aprendeu a fundo a organização e a prática da fiação. Sabendo do interesse americano por máquinas assim, e da lei que proibia levar os projetos para fora, memorizou tudo o que conseguiu e embarcou para Nova York. Em Rhode Island, o industrial Moses Brown tinha comprado uma máquina "no padrão de Arkwright" que ninguém conseguia pôr para funcionar. Slater escreveu oferecendo seus serviços, com uma promessa: se não fizesse fio tão bom quanto o inglês, não cobraria nada e jogaria tudo da ponte. Como não havia mecânicos no país, encontrou Oziel Wilkinson e o filho David para fundir e forjar as peças de ferro, e reconstruiu as máquinas movidas a água com base no que tinha memorizado. Historiadores discutem o quanto foi memória pura, já que ele contou com ajuda e com a máquina comprada por Brown. Em 1793, ele e Brown abriram a primeira fábrica em Pawtucket, a primeira fiação hidráulica bem-sucedida dos EUA. Os primeiros empregados eram crianças de sete a 12 anos. Nos EUA, Andrew Jackson o chamou de "pai da Revolução Industrial americana"; em Belper, alguns viram traição à cidade que vivia das fábricas de Strutt.

fontes.trecho: was an early English-American industrialist known as the "Father of the American Industrial Revolution", a phrase coined by Andrew Jackson [...] In the United Kingdom, he was called "Slater the Traitor" and "Sam the Slate" because he brought British textile technology to the United States [...] He memorized the textile factory machinery designs as an apprentice to a pioneer in the British industry before migrating to the U.S. at the age of 21. [...] At age ten, he began work at the cotton mill opened that year by Jedediah Strutt using the water frame pioneered by Richard Arkwright at nearby Cromford Mill. [...] Slater was well trained by Strutt and, by age 21, he had gained a thorough knowledge of the organization and practice of cotton spinning. He learned of the American interest in developing similar machines, and he was also aware of British law against exporting the designs. He memorized as much as he could, and departed for New York City in 1789. Some people of Belper called him "Slater the Traitor", as they considered his move a betrayal of the town where many earned their living at Strutt's mills. [...] In August 1789, they acquired a 32-spindle frame "after the Arkwright pattern" but could not operate it. At this point, Slater wrote to them, offering his services. [...] He promised: "If I do not make as good yarn, as they do in England, I will have nothing for my services but will throw the whole of what I have attempted over the bridge." [...] Slater found no mechanics in the U.S. when he arrived and had great difficulty finding someone to build the machinery. Eventually, he located Oziel Wilkinson and his son, David, to produce iron castings and forgings for the machinery. [...] He was able to single-handedly construct from memory the water-powered spinning machinery. [...] In 1793, Slater and Brown opened their first factory in Pawtucket. [...] The result was the first successful water-powered roller spinning textile mill in the U.S. [...] Children aged seven to 12 were the first employees of the mill

fontes.titulo: The Making of a Hero: Samuel Slater and the Arkwright Frames (Rhode Island Historical Society)
fontes.trecho: Disputes the idea that Slater worked "strictly from memory" and without significant assistance

gancho: No fim de 1862, com as fábricas de algodão do norte da Inglaterra paradas e operários na miséria, trabalhadores reunidos em Manchester declararam apoio a Lincoln contra a escravidão. Ele respondeu com uma carta.
explicacao: A crise ficou conhecida como a Fome do Algodão, de 1861 a 1865, e não teve uma causa só. Os anos de 1859 e 1860 tinham produzido mais tecido do que se conseguia vender, e a Guerra Civil americana interrompeu a chegada do algodão, enquanto especuladores seguravam os estoques. O preço do algodão bruto subiu várias centenas por cento, e os operários de Lancashire passaram de mais bem pagos a mais pobres da Grã-Bretanha. Em Stalybridge, no inverno de 1862–1863, só cinco das 39 fábricas da cidade davam trabalho em tempo integral. A opinião estava longe de ser unânime: muitos donos de fábrica e operários se ressentiam do bloqueio da União, e bandeiras confederadas tremulavam em várias cidades algodoeiras. Mesmo assim, em 31 de dezembro de 1862, uma reunião de trabalhadores no Free Trade Hall, em Manchester, decidiu apoiar a União na luta contra a escravidão e escreveu a Lincoln. Em 19 de janeiro de 1863, ele agradeceu, lamentou o sofrimento deles e chamou o gesto de exemplo de "sublime heroísmo cristão". Dos Estados Unidos chegaram navios com comida para Lancashire, e um monumento em Manchester reproduz trechos das duas cartas.

fontes.trecho: The Lancashire Cotton Famine, also known as the Cotton Famine or the Cotton Panic (1861–1865), was a depression in the textile industry of North West England, brought about by overproduction in a time of contracting world markets. It coincided with the interruption of baled cotton imports caused by the American Civil War and speculators buying up new stock for storage [...] The boom years of 1859 and 1860 had produced more woven cotton than could be sold [...] The price for raw cotton increased by several hundred percent due to blockade and lack of imports. [...] workers became unemployed and went from being the most prosperous workers in Britain to the most impoverished. [...] By the winter of 1862–1863 there were 7,000 unemployed operatives in Stalybridge, one of the worst affected towns. Only five of the town's 39 factories and 24 machine shops were employing people full-time. [...] Many mill owners and workers resented the blockade and continued to see the war as an issue of tariffs against free trade. [...] Confederate flags were flown in many cotton towns. On 31 December 1862, a meeting of cotton workers at the Free Trade Hall in Manchester, despite their increasing hardship, resolved to support the Union in its fight against slavery. [...] On 19 January 1863, Abraham Lincoln sent an address thanking the cotton workers of Lancashire for their support [...] I know and deeply deplore the sufferings which the workingmen at Manchester and in all Europe are called to endure in this crisis. [...] I cannot but regard your decisive utterance upon the question as an instance of sublime Christian heroism which has not been surpassed in any age or in any country. [...] A monument in Brazenose Street, Lincoln Square, Manchester, commemorates the events and reproduces portions of both documents. [...] The Federal American government sent a gift of food to the people of Lancashire.

gancho: O fósforo branco dos fósforos do século XIX podia destruir a mandíbula de quem os fabricava, e o osso doente brilhava no escuro. Uma grande fábrica de Londres já fazia fósforos seguros, mas eles custavam mais.
explicacao: A doença, chamada em inglês de phossy jaw, vinha de respirar o vapor do fósforo branco, sobretudo quando a mistura era aquecida. Começava com dor de dente e inchaço na gengiva e evoluía para perda dos dentes, abscessos e necrose do osso; a mortalidade relatada era de cerca de 20%. A Bryant & May, em Londres, conhecia o problema: quem reclamasse de dor de dente era mandado arrancar os dentes na hora, sob pena de demissão. A empresa importava da Suécia fósforos de segurança, feitos com fósforo vermelho, desde 1850, e chegou a fabricá-los a partir de 1855, mas eles não competiam em preço com os de fósforo branco. Em julho de 1888, cerca de 1.400 mulheres e meninas da fábrica de Bow cruzaram os braços depois da demissão de uma colega. Venceram: as multas e descontos injustos foram abolidos, e as refeições passaram a ser feitas numa sala separada, longe do fósforo. Em 1891, o Exército da Salvação abriu uma fábrica com fósforo vermelho, mas seus fósforos custavam de início o triplo. O fósforo branco só foi banido dos fósforos britânicos por uma lei de 1908, que aplicava a Convenção de Berna, de 1906.

fontes.trecho: In July 1888 the women and teenage girls working at the Bryant & May match factory in Bow, London, England went on strike. [...] Phossy jaw developed by inhalation of phosphorus vapour—particularly when the ingredient was heated—which caused osteonecrosis of the jaw bone. This manifested itself in, initially, toothaches and flu-like symptoms, then tooth loss, abscesses, swelling of the gums, the formation of fistula and necrosis of the jaw. Mortality was reported in around 20 per cent of cases. [...] Bryant & May were aware of phossy jaw. If a worker complained of having toothache, they were told to have the teeth removed immediately or be sacked. [...] This caused management to dismiss a worker (on some other pretext), on or about 2 July 1888, which set off the strike. Approximately 1,400 women and girls refused to work by the end of the first day after the dismissal. [...] in which fines, deductions for the cost of materials and other unfair deductions would be abolished. [...] An important additional term was that meals were to be taken in a separate room, where the food would not be contaminated with phosphorus. [...] In 1891 the Salvation Army opened up its own match factory in the Bow district of London, using less toxic red phosphorus and paying better wages. [...] The owners, Francis May and William Bryant, had started importing red-phosphorus based safety matches from John Edvard Lundström, in Sweden, in 1850. [...] They started using red phosphorus in 1855, but could not compete in price against the much cheaper white phosphorus-based matches [...] their own matches were initially three times the price of white phosphorus-based matches. [...] prohibiting the use of white phosphorus in matches after 31 December 1910. This was the United Kingdom's implementation of the 1906 Berne Convention on the prohibition of white phosphorus in matches.

It was caused by white phosphorus vapor, which destroys the bones of the jaw. [...] Affected bones glowed a greenish-white colour in the dark. [...] In Great Britain, a ban on white phosphorus matches was introduced by the White Phosphorus Matches Prohibition Act 1908

gancho: Friedrich Engels, coautor do Manifesto Comunista, trabalhou quase vinte anos na firma de algodão da família em Manchester, chegou a sócio e, com esse dinheiro, sustentou Karl Marx enquanto ele preparava O Capital.
explicacao: Engels era o filho mais velho de um próspero dono de fiação da Prússia. Em 1842, o pai o mandou a Manchester para trabalhar no escritório de uma fábrica da Ermen & Engels, em parte para afastá-lo da política radical. Teve o efeito oposto: a cidade, símbolo da Revolução Industrial, deu a ele o material para o livro A Situação da Classe Trabalhadora na Inglaterra, de 1845. Depois das revoluções de 1848, com a família de Marx na miséria em Londres, Engels voltou à firma em 1850 para poder ajudá-los. Levou uma vida dupla. Em público, era um comerciante respeitável, membro da Bolsa e de clubes exclusivos, que caçava raposas com uma das caçadas mais aristocráticas da Inglaterra. Em segredo, vivia com a irlandesa Mary Burns, da classe operária, em bairros pobres. Em 1860 já ganhava mais de mil libras por ano, e em 1864 virou sócio. Ao longo de vinte anos, mandou aos Marx entre 3 mil e 4 mil libras, o que na prática bancou a pesquisa e a escrita de O Capital. Também serviu de fonte para o livro, com dados de dentro da indústria, como custos de máquinas, contabilidade e o funcionamento do mercado do algodão.

fontes.trecho: They became active in the Communist League, which commissioned them to write the Manifesto. [...] In 1842, his father sent him to Manchester, England, to work in a cotton mill in which the family had an investment. His experiences of the industrial working class there led him to write his first major work, The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). [...] Engels participated actively in the Revolutions of 1848, including in armed combat, before being forced into exile in England. From 1850, he lived in Manchester and worked for the family firm of Ermen & Engels for two decades, leading a double life as a respectable cotton merchant while providing crucial financial support to the impoverished Marx family in London. [...] He was the eldest of nine children born to Friedrich Engels Sr., a prosperous cotton mill owner [...] Engels's father sent him to Manchester to work as a clerk in the office of Ermen & Engels's Victoria Mill in Weaste, Salford. This move, intended to steer him away from radical politics, had the opposite effect. Manchester, the "shock-city" of the Industrial Revolution, provided Engels with the empirical evidence for the communist theories he had absorbed in Germany. [...] In November 1850, reconciling with his family, he agreed to return to Manchester and resume his position at the Ermen & Engels office to provide financial support for Marx. [...] he endured this "purgatory" for nearly twenty years. [...] rose through the ranks, becoming a partner in the firm in 1864. His income grew substantially, reaching over £1,000 a year by 1860 [...] Over twenty years, he sent a constant stream of funds to the Marx family in London, totalling between £3,000 and £4,000, effectively funding Marx's research and the writing of Das Kapital. [...] He maintained an official residence in respectable city suburbs while living secretly with Mary Burns, and later her sister Lizzy, in a series of modest houses in working-class districts like Chorlton and Ardwick. In his public life, Engels became a stalwart of Manchester society. He was a member of the Royal Exchange [...] and exclusive gentlemen's clubs like the Albert Club and the Brazenose Club. A passionate equestrian, he regularly rode with the Cheshire Hounds, one of the most aristocratic fox hunts in England [...] He provided detailed, real-world information on the workings of capitalist industry, from machinery costs and bookkeeping practices to the structure of the cotton market [...] the Irish working-class sisters Mary (c. 1822–1863) and Lizzy Burns

gancho: O Motim do Chá de Boston, em 1773, não foi um protesto contra chá caro. A lei que o provocou deixava o chá legal mais barato, a ponto de custar menos que o contrabandeado.
explicacao: Em 1773, a Companhia Britânica das Índias Orientais estava perto da falência, com montanhas de chá encalhado nos armazéns de Londres. Nas Treze Colônias, a maior parte do chá vinha de contrabando holandês, que não pagava impostos: cerca de 86% do total, segundo uma estimativa. A Lei do Chá, aprovada naquele ano, deixou a companhia mandar o produto direto para a América, sem intermediários e sem os tributos cobrados na Grã-Bretanha. Com isso, a libra-peso do chá legal, que custava uns 3 xelins, poderia ser vendida por 2, abaixo dos 2 xelins e 1 pêni cobrados pelos contrabandistas. O pulo do gato estava no que a lei mantinha: um imposto de 3 pence por libra recolhido nas colônias. Comprando o chá mais barato, os colonos aceitariam na prática o direito do Parlamento de taxá-los. A resistência juntou quem defendia o princípio de "nenhum imposto sem representação" e comerciantes, alguns deles contrabandistas, que seriam arruinados pela concorrência. Em 16 de dezembro de 1773, colonos, alguns disfarçados de indígenas, subiram nos navios ancorados em Boston e jogaram ao mar 340 ou 342 caixas de chá. As punições britânicas que vieram depois aumentaram a tensão que desembocou na guerra de independência.

fontes.trecho: The protest movement that culminated with the Boston Tea Party was not a dispute about high taxes. The price of legally imported tea was actually reduced by the Tea Act of 1773. [...] The familiar "no taxation without representation" argument [...] In 1772, legally imported Bohea, the most common variety of tea, sold for about 3 shillings (3s) per pound [...] After the Tea Act, colonial consignees would be able to sell tea for 2 shillings per pound (2s), just under the smugglers' price of 2 shillings and 1 penny (2s 1d). [...] its hidden purpose was to force the colonists to pay a tax of 3 pennies on every pound of tea. [...] Colonial merchants, some of them smugglers, played a significant role in the protests. Because the Tea Act made legally imported tea cheaper, it threatened to put smugglers of Dutch tea out of business. [...] threw 340 or 342 chests into Boston Harbor.

The principal objective was to reduce the massive amount of tea held by the financially troubled British East India Company in its London warehouses [...] approximately 86% of all the tea in America at the time was smuggled Dutch tea. The act granted the company the right to directly ship its tea to North America and the right to the duty-free export of tea from Britain, although the tax imposed by the Townshend Acts and collected in the colonies remained in force. [...] In Boston, this resistance culminated in the Boston Tea Party on December 16, 1773, when colonists (some disguised as Native Americans) boarded tea ships anchored in the harbour and dumped their tea cargo overboard. [...] These actions further raised tensions that led to the eruption of the American War of Independence [...] Colonists would willingly pay for cheaper Company tea, on which the Townshend tax was still collected, thus legitimizing Parliament's ability to tax the colonies.

gancho: John Adams e Thomas Jefferson, líderes da independência dos EUA, morreram no mesmo dia: 4 de julho de 1826, 50 anos após a Declaração. Adams teria dito no fim: "Jefferson sobrevive". Errou por horas.
explicacao: Os dois estiveram juntos no Congresso que aprovou a Declaração de Independência. Anos depois, Jefferson chamaria Adams de "pilar" da defesa do texto no plenário. Depois veio a política. Adams foi o segundo presidente dos EUA, e Jefferson, seu vice-presidente. Na eleição de 1800, Jefferson, então descrito como ex-amigo, derrotou Adams. Desde que Adams deixou o cargo, as casas dos dois ficaram sem contato até 1812, tirando uma breve troca de cartas entre Jefferson e Abigail, mulher de Adams, que logo descambou para a briga política. No início de 1812, o médico Benjamin Rush, amigo dos dois, incentivou a reaproximação. Adams mandou um bilhete amistoso no Ano-Novo, Jefferson respondeu na hora com uma carta cordial, e a amizade renasceu pelo correio. As cartas seguiram até o fim da vida deles e são tidas como um dos grandes legados da literatura americana. Em 4 de julho de 1826, exatos 50 anos depois da aprovação da Declaração, Adams morreu de um ataque cardíaco em casa, por volta das 6 e 20 da tarde, aos 90 anos. Segundo relatos, entre suas últimas palavras estava o nome do amigo e rival, numa frase registrada como "Thomas Jefferson sobrevive". Não sabia que Jefferson tinha morrido várias horas antes.

fontes.trecho: John Adams (October 30, 1735 – July 4, 1826) was a Founding Father and the second president of the United States from 1797 to 1801. [...] Adams was the first vice president of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797. [...] In his 1800 bid for reelection to the presidency, opposition from Federalists and accusations of despotism from Jeffersonians led to Adams losing to his vice president and former friend, Thomas Jefferson. [...] Jefferson hailed Adams as "the pillar of [the Declaration's] support on the floor of Congress, [its] ablest advocate and defender against the multifarious assaults it encountered." [...] Congress approved the Declaration of Independence on July 4. [...] This initiated a brief correspondence between the two which quickly descended into political rancor. Jefferson terminated it by not replying to Abigail's fourth letter. Aside from that, by 1812 there had been no communication between Monticello, the home of Jefferson, and Peacefield since Adams left office. In early 1812, Adams reconciled with Jefferson. [...] Their mutual friend Benjamin Rush, who had been corresponding with both, encouraged them to reach out to each other. On New Year's Day, Adams sent a brief, friendly note to Jefferson [...] Jefferson replied immediately with a cordial letter, and the two revived their friendship, which they sustained by mail. Their correspondence lasted the rest of their lives, and has been hailed as among the great legacies of American literature. [...] On July 4, 1826, the 50th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration of Independence, Adams died of a heart attack at Peacefield at approximately 6:20 pm. His last words included an acknowledgement of his longtime friend and rival: "Thomas Jefferson survives." Adams was unaware that Jefferson had died several hours before. At 90, Adams was the longest-lived US president

gancho: Quando a Bastilha foi tomada, em 1789, havia só sete presos lá dentro, e a fortaleza já estava marcada para demolição. O que a multidão exigia eram as armas e a pólvora guardadas ali.
explicacao: Antes de chegar à Bastilha, em 14 de julho de 1789, os revolucionários de Paris tinham invadido o Hôtel des Invalides atrás de armas e levado de 29 mil a 32 mil mosquetes, mas sem pólvora nem munição. Dias antes, o comandante dos Invalides transferira 250 barris de pólvora para a Bastilha, que parecia um lugar mais seguro. A multidão se juntou diante da fortaleza pedindo que os canhões fossem recuados e que as armas e a pólvora fossem liberadas. Depois de quatro horas de luta e 94 mortos, os insurgentes entraram. A Bastilha era um símbolo do poder do rei, mas quase não funcionava mais como prisão: lá estavam quatro falsificadores, dois homens tidos como loucos e um conde preso a pedido da própria família. O Marquês de Sade, que também estivera preso ali, tinha sido transferido dez dias antes, depois de gritar a quem passava na rua que os presos estavam sendo massacrados. Manter a velha fortaleza custava caro, e pouco antes já se decidira trocá-la por um espaço público. Depois da queda, ela foi demolida em cinco meses, e o empreiteiro da demolição vendeu réplicas esculpidas em tijolos dela. Lafayette deu a chave da Bastilha a George Washington, e ela continua exposta em Mount Vernon, a casa dele.

fontes.trecho: which occurred in Paris, France, on 14 July 1789 [...] After four hours of fighting and 94 deaths, the insurgents were able to enter the Bastille. [...] The prison contained only seven inmates at the time of its storming and was already scheduled for demolition but was seen by the revolutionaries as a symbol of the monarchy's abuse of power. [...] had earlier stormed the Hôtel des Invalides without meeting significant opposition. Their intention had been to gather the weapons held there (29,000 to 32,000 muskets, but without powder or shot). The commandant at the Invalides had in the previous few days taken the precaution of transferring 250 barrels of gunpowder to the Bastille for safer storage. [...] four forgers arrested under warrants issued by the Grand Châtelet court; James F.X. Whyte, an Irish born "lunatic" [...] A previous prisoner the Marquis de Sade had been transferred out ten days earlier, after shouting to passers-by that the prisoners were being massacred. The high cost of maintaining a garrisoned medieval fortress, for what was seen as having a limited purpose, had led to a decision being made shortly before the disturbances began to replace it with an open public space [...] calling for the pulling back of the seemingly threatening cannon from the embrasures of the towers and walls and the release of the arms and gunpowder stored inside. [...] the prison contained only seven inmates: four forgers, two mentally ill men, and a count imprisoned at his family's request. [...] were all carried out within five months. In 1790, Lafayette gave the key to the Bastille—weighing one pound three ounces—to U.S. President George Washington. [...] The key remains on display at Washington's residence of Mount Vernon. Palloy took bricks from the Bastille and had them carved into replicas of the fortress, which he sold

gancho: No calendário da Revolução Francesa, a semana tinha dez dias, e cada dia ganhou nome de planta, bicho, mineral ou ferramenta. Os trabalhadores reclamaram da folga a cada dez dias, embora descansassem mais no ano.
explicacao: O calendário republicano foi adotado em 1793 e usado pelo governo francês por cerca de 12 anos. Tinha 12 meses de 30 dias, cada um dividido em três "décadas" de dez dias, mais cinco ou seis dias de festa no fim do ano. Os meses tinham nomes ligados ao clima e ao campo, como Brumário, da névoa, e Termidor, do calor do verão. A ideia era apagar a influência da Igreja e da monarquia. No calendário católico, cada dia era dedicado a um santo; o poeta Fabre d'Églantine, que inventou os nomes dos meses, deu a cada dia um nome tirado da vida rural. Os dias terminados em 5 levavam o nome de um animal, os terminados em 0, o de uma ferramenta agrícola, e os demais, nomes de plantas, exceto no Nivoso, o primeiro mês do inverno, em que eram minerais. O décimo dia, o décadi, substituiu o domingo como dia de descanso, e por um tempo os casamentos só podiam ser celebrados nele. A semana de dez dias desagradou aos trabalhadores, que passaram a ter um dia livre a cada dez, e não a cada sete, embora ganhassem também meia folga no quíntidi, o quinto dia, o que somava 54 dias livres por ano, contra os 52 ou 53 domingos de antes; e acabou suprimida antes do resto. Napoleão aboliu o calendário em 1806. Fabre não viu o fim: foi guilhotinado em 1794, acusado de falsificação num caso de corrupção ligado à Companhia Francesa das Índias Orientais.

fontes.trecho: used by the French government for about 12 years from late 1793 to 1805 [...] The calendar consisted of twelve 30-day months, each divided into three 10-day cycles similar to weeks, plus five or six intercalary days at the end to fill out the balance of a solar year. It was designed in part to remove all religious and royalist influences from the calendar [...] the republican calendar continued to be used until 1 January 1806, when Napoleon declared it abolished. [...] poet, actor and playwright Fabre d'Églantine (who invented the names of the months) [...] The month names were based on nature, principally having to do with the prevailing weather in and around Paris [...] Brumaire (from French brume 'mist' [...] Thermidor (from Greek θέρμη, thermē, 'summer heat') [...] Décadis became an official day of rest instead of Sunday, in order to diminish the influence of the Roman Catholic Church. [...] required that marriages must only be celebrated on décadis. [...] The Roman Catholic Church used a calendar of saints, which named each day of the year after an associated saint. To reduce the influence of the Church, Fabre d'Églantine introduced a rural calendar in which each day of the year had a unique name associated with the rural economy [...] Every décadi (ending in 0) was named after an agricultural tool. Each quintidi (ending in 5) was named for a common animal. The rest of the days were named for "grain, pasture, trees, roots, flowers, fruits" and other plants, except for the first month of winter, Nivôse, during which the rest of the days were named after minerals. [...] the 10-day décade was unpopular and had already been suppressed three years earlier in favor of the seven-day week [...] The 10-day décade was unpopular with laborers because they received only one full day of rest out of ten, instead of one in seven [...] although they also got a half-day off on the fifth day (thus 36 full days and 36 half days in a year, for a total of 54 free days, compared to the usual 52 or 53 Sundays)

On 12 January 1794 Fabre was arrested by order of the Committee of Public Safety on a charge of malversation and forgery in connection with the affairs of the French East India Company. [...] Fabre died under the guillotine on 5 April 1794 with the other Dantonists.

gancho: A Revolução Francesa tentou decimalizar até o relógio: dias de 10 horas, horas de 100 minutos. Meio-dia virou "cinco horas". Fizeram relógios assim, mas a obrigação durou pouco mais de seis meses.
explicacao: Junto com o metro e o calendário republicano, os revolucionários quiseram aplicar a base 10 também à hora do dia. O dia passou a ter 10 horas decimais, cada uma com 100 minutos decimais de 100 segundos decimais, num total de 100.000 segundos por dia. A hora nova equivalia a 144 minutos comuns, e o segundo novo, a 0,864 segundo comum. Na contagem, meia-noite era "dez horas" e meio-dia, "cinco horas". Foram fabricados relógios de parede e de bolso com mostradores que exibiam as duas contagens, a tradicional e a decimal. Mas o sistema não pegou. O uso nos registros públicos só passou a valer em 22 de setembro de 1794, e a obrigatoriedade foi suspensa em 7 de abril de 1795, pela mesma lei que instituiu o sistema métrico. Um dos argumentos contra era que a mudança não trazia vantagem clara para quase ninguém e ainda poderia prejudicar a aceitação das novas medidas. Algumas cidades insistiram por mais tempo: em Toulouse, um relógio decimal que só tinha o ponteiro das horas ficou cinco anos na fachada do Capitólio. A divisão decimal acabou útil mesmo para os astrônomos, e a França ainda faria outra tentativa de decimalizar o tempo em 1897.

fontes.trecho: French Republican calendar time system used from 1794 to 1800, during the French Revolution, which divided the day into 10 decimal hours, each decimal hour into 100 decimal minutes and each decimal minute into 100 decimal seconds (100,000 decimal seconds per day) [...] Thus, midnight was called dix heures ("ten hours"), noon was called cinq heures ("five hours"), etc. [...] Although clocks and watches were produced with faces showing both standard time with numbers 1–24 and decimal time with numbers 1–10, decimal time never caught on; it was not used for public records until the beginning of the Republican year III, 22 September 1794, and mandatory use was suspended 7 April 1795 (18 Germinal of the Year III). In spite of this, decimal time was used in many cities, including Marseille and Toulouse, where a decimal clock with just an hour hand was on the front of the Capitole for five years. [...] As it does not offer almost all of the nation any marked advantage, it would only throw a disadvantage on the new system of measures and the decimal method [...] Thus, the law of 18 Germinal An III (April 7, 1795) establishing the metric system, rather than including metric units for time, repealed the mandatory use of decimal time, although its use continued for a number of years in some places. As predicted, it was quickly found to be useful by astrono [...] The French made another attempt at the decimalization of time in 1897

Thus an hour was 144 conventional minutes (2.4 times as long as a conventional hour), a minute was 86.4 conventional seconds (44% longer than a conventional minute), and a second was 0.864 conventional seconds (13.6% shorter than a conventional second). Clocks were manufactured to display this decimal time, but it did not catch on.

gancho: O metro nasceu na Revolução Francesa, de uma medição da Terra entre Dunquerque e Barcelona. Um dos astrônomos encarregados chegou a ser preso porque desconfiaram que seus instrumentos fossem armas.
explicacao: Em 1790, a Assembleia revolucionária pediu à Academia de Ciências medidas novas, baseadas na natureza. A comissão descartou o pêndulo que bate o segundo, porque o comprimento dele muda com a gravidade de cada lugar, e decidiu que o metro seria a décima milionésima parte da distância entre o Polo Norte e o Equador, medida ao longo do meridiano de Paris. Os astrônomos Jean-Baptiste Delambre e Pierre Méchain mediram então o arco entre Dunquerque e Barcelona. Méchain, que começou o trecho sul em 1791, sofreu com a revolução: foi preso sob suspeita de que seus instrumentos fossem armas, ficou retido em Barcelona quando estourou a guerra entre França e Espanha e teve os bens em Paris confiscados durante o Terror. Ao conferir a latitude pelas estrelas, encontrou resultados anômalos e passou a duvidar da própria precisão. A análise dos números dele mostra que ele manteve as discrepâncias sempre minúsculas, o que fez suas medições parecerem mais precisas do que seria razoável com equipamento do século XVIII. As dúvidas o levaram de volta à Espanha em 1804, onde morreu de febre amarela. Hoje se sabe que o metro ficou 0,197 milímetro mais curto do que a definição original pretendia, sobretudo por causa de um desvio da vertical no extremo sul da medição. O suposto erro de Méchain não afetou o valor final.

fontes.trecho: the determination of the southern part of the meridian arc of the Earth's surface between Dunkirk and Barcelona beginning in 1791. This measurement would become the basis of the metric system's unit of length, the meter. He encountered numerous difficulties on this project, largely stemming from the effects of the French Revolution. He was arrested after it was suspected his instruments were weapons, he was interned in Barcelona after war broke out between France and Spain, and his property in Paris was confiscated during The Terror. [...] Méchain was uncertain of the precision of his measurements owing to anomalous results in verifying his latitude by astronomical observation. [...] Méchain consistently kept the discrepancy very tiny, essentially forcing his individual reported measurements to appear more precise and consistent than would be reasonably expected of a survey involving more than a hundred measurements of mostly rough country using 18th-century equipment; Méchain's putative error did not affect the final value of the length of the metre nor the measurement of the meridian. [...] Continuing doubts about his measurements of the Dunkirk-Barcelona arc led him to return to that work. This took him back to Spain in 1804, where he caught yellow fever and died

In 1790, during the French Revolution, the National Convention tasked the French Academy of Sciences with reforming the units of measurement. The Academy formed a commission, which rejected using the pendulum as a unit of length and decided that the new measure should be equal to one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator [...] This was to be measured along the meridian passing through the centre of Paris Observatory. [...] this was rejected as it had been discovered that this length varied from place to place with local gravity. [...] Following the arc measurement of Delambre and Méchain [...] we now know that the metre is 0.197 millimetres shorter than it should be according to its original proposed definition, mainly due to not taking into account a vertical deflection in the southern end of the arc measurement of Delambre and Méchain.

gancho: Lavoisier, o químico que batizou o oxigênio, recomendou à empresa de impostos de que era sócio pôr 6,3% de água no tabaco. Na Revolução, uma das acusações que o levaram à guilhotina foi molhar o tabaco.
explicacao: Antoine Lavoisier financiava sua ciência com a Ferme générale, uma companhia que adiantava ao rei a receita prevista dos impostos e, em troca, ganhava o direito de cobrá-los. Ela detinha o monopólio do tabaco na França e era uma das instituições mais odiadas do Antigo Regime. Lavoisier estudou as fraudes dos vendedores, que misturavam cinza e água ao tabaco, e notou que muita água fazia o fumo fermentar e cheirar mal, mas um pouco melhorava o produto. Por recomendação dele, as fábricas passaram a acrescentar 6,3% de água, e, para compensar, a companhia entregava 17 onças de tabaco cobrando 16. Veio a Revolução. Em 1793, foi ordenada a prisão de todos os antigos cobradores, acusados de fraudar o Estado e de pôr água no tabaco antes de vendê-lo. Lavoisier redigiu a defesa, mas o tribunal via na condenação um jeito de confiscar fortunas para o Estado. Ele foi guilhotinado em 8 de maio de 1794, aos 50 anos, com outros 27 réus. A frase atribuída ao juiz, "a República não precisa de sábios", vem de uma lenda popular. Um ano e meio depois, o governo francês o inocentou, e os bens foram entregues à viúva com um bilhete: "À viúva de Lavoisier, que foi falsamente condenado".

fontes.trecho: He named oxygen (1778) [...] The Ferme générale was one of the most hated components of the Ancien Régime [...] All of these political and economic activities enabled him to fund his scientific research. [...] a tax farming financial company which advanced the estimated tax revenue to the royal government in return for the right to collect the taxes. [...] The Farmers General held a monopoly of the production, import and sale of tobacco in France [...] adulterated, most commonly with ash and water. [...] Lavoisier also found that while adding a lot of water to bulk the tobacco up would cause it to ferment and smell bad, the addition of a very small amount improved the product. Thereafter the factories of the Farmers General added, as he recommended, a consistent 6.3% of water by volume to the tobacco they processed. To allow for this addition, the Farmers General delivered to retailers seventeen ounces of tobacco while only charging for sixteen. [...] On 24 November 1793, the arrest of all the former tax farmers was ordered. Lavoisier and the other Farmers General faced nine accusations of defrauding the state of money owed to it, and of adding water to tobacco before selling it. Lavoisier drafted their defense [...] The court, however, was inclined to believe that by condemning them and seizing the goods of the Farmers General, it would recover huge sums for the state. Lavoisier was convicted and guillotined on 8 May 1794 in Paris, at the age of 50, along with his 27 co-defendants. According to popular legend, the appeal to spare his life, in order that he could continue his experiments, was cut short by the judge, Coffinhal: "La République n'a pas besoin de savants ni de chimistes; le cours de la justice ne peut être suspendu." [...] A year and a half after his execution, Lavoisier was completely exonerated by the French government. During the White Terror, his belongings were delivered to his widow. A brief note was included, reading "To the widow of Lavoisier, who was falsely convicted".

gancho: O médico que deu nome à guilhotina era contra a pena de morte e só queria execuções menos cruéis. A máquina, estreada em 1792, decapitou alguém na França pela última vez em 1977.
explicacao: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin não inventou o aparelho: o protótipo foi obra de outro médico, Antoine Louis. Deputado em 1789, Guillotin tentou abolir a pena de morte e não conseguiu. Na época, a decapitação com machado ou espada era privilégio dos nobres e nem sempre matava na hora, enquanto os plebeus eram enforcados, queimados ou mortos na roda. Ele propôs então que todo condenado, de qualquer classe, fosse decapitado por um mecanismo simples, esperando que uma morte rápida fosse o primeiro passo para o fim das execuções e atraísse multidões menores. Uma frase atribuída a ele, de que a máquina cortaria a cabeça "num piscar de olhos" sem que a pessoa sentisse nada, virou piada e canção cômica, e o nome dele grudou no aparelho. Guillotin lamentou isso pelo resto da vida. A família pediu ao governo que rebatizasse a máquina e, diante da recusa, trocou o próprio sobrenome. Ao contrário do que muitos dizem, ele não morreu guilhotinado: morreu em casa, de causas naturais, em 1814. Quem passou pela lâmina foi um médico de Lyon com o mesmo sobrenome. A guilhotina seguiu em uso por quase dois séculos. A última execução foi a de Hamida Djandoubi, em Marselha, em 10 de setembro de 1977, também a última decapitação legal do mundo ocidental. A França aboliu a pena de morte em 1981.

fontes.trecho: Although he did not invent the guillotine and opposed the death penalty, his name became an eponym for it. The actual inventor of the prototype was a French physician, Antoine Louis. [...] On 2 May 1789, he became one of 10 Paris deputies in the Estates-General of 1789 [...] His experiences as a doctor had led him to oppose capital punishment: at first, he attempted to abolish it, but was unsuccessful. At that time, beheading in France was typically by axe or sword, which did not always cause immediate death. Additionally, beheading was reserved for the nobility, while commoners were typically hanged [...] Other methods included burning at the stake, the breaking wheel [...] All punishments for the same class of crime shall be the same, regardless of the criminal [...] Guillotin was opposed to the death penalty, and hoped that a more humane and less painful method of execution would be the first step towards total abolition. He also hoped that, as the decapitation machine would kill quickly without prolonged suffering, this would reduce the size and enthusiasm of crowds that often witnessed executions. [...] He was quoted (or possibly misquoted) as saying, "Now, with my machine, I cut off your head in the twinkling of an eye, and you never feel it!" The statement quickly became a popular joke, and a few days after the debate a comic song about Guillotin and "his" machine circulated, forever tying his name to it [...] the first executions using it took place on 25 April 1792. [...] for the remainder of his life, he deeply regretted that the machine was named after him. [...] The association with the guillotine so embarrassed Guillotin's family that they petitioned the French government to rename it; when the government refused, they instead changed their own family name. By coincidence, another person named Guillotin was indeed executed by the guillotine – he was J.M.V. Guillotin, a doctor of Lyon. This coincidence may have contributed to erroneous statements that J-I Guillotin was put to death on the machine that bears his name; however, in reality, Guillotin died at home in Paris in 1814 of natural causes

Djandoubi was the last person to be executed in France before the abolition of capital punishment in 1981, and the last person to be lawfully executed by beheading anywhere in the Western world. [...] On 10 September 1977 [...] Djandoubi was executed by guillotine at Baumettes Prison in Marseille.

gancho: Para reconhecer o Haiti, a França exigiu, com navios de guerra, 150 milhões de francos de indenização pelos bens perdidos, incluindo os escravizados. Segundo o New York Times, a conta só se encerrou em 1947.
explicacao: São Domingos, hoje Haiti, era a colônia europeia mais lucrativa do mundo. Seu açúcar respondia por 40% do mercado do Atlântico, e em 1790 viviam ali 425 mil escravizados. Em 1804, depois de uma grande revolta de escravizados, o país declarou independência. Veio o isolamento: nenhum Estado aceitava comerciar com ele, e os EUA, com medo de que o exemplo inspirasse seus próprios escravizados, só reconheceram o Haiti em 1862. Em 1825, navios de guerra franceses levaram a exigência: 150 milhões de francos, em cinco parcelas anuais de 30 milhões, para compensar os antigos proprietários pelas perdas da revolução, contando como propriedade as pessoas escravizadas. Em troca, a França reconheceria o novo país. O Haiti precisou de um empréstimo para pagar a primeira parcela, e em 1838 a França reduziu o restante para 60 milhões. Para quitar uma dívida, o país tomava outra, e uma análise publicada pelo New York Times em 2022 concluiu que o último pagamento ligado a esses empréstimos só foi feito em 1947. O jornal estimou que o Haiti pagou de fato cerca de 112 milhões de francos de indenização, algo como 560 milhões de dólares de 2022. Em 2016, o Parlamento francês revogou a ordem de 1825, mas nenhuma reparação foi oferecida.

fontes.trecho: involves an 1825 agreement between Haiti and France that included France demanding an indemnity of 150 million francs in five annual payments of 30 million to be paid by Haiti in claims over property, including Haitian slaves, that was lost through the Haitian Revolution in return for diplomatic recognition. Haiti was forced to take a loan for the first 30 million, and in 1838 France agreed to reduce the remaining debt to 60 million to be paid over 30 years, with the final payment paid in 1883. However, according to a 2022 The New York Times analysis, because of other loans taken to pay off this loan, the final payment to debtors was actually made in 1947. They approximated that 112 million francs was actually paid in indemnity, which is equivalent to $560 million in 2022 after adjusting for inflation. Restoration France's demand of payments in exchange for recognizing Haiti's independence was delivered to the country by several French warships in 1825 [...] In 2016, the Parliament of France repealed the 1825 ordinance of Charles X, though no reparations have been offered by France. [...] Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, was the most profitable and productive European colony in the world going into the 1800s. [...] The Saint-Domingue population reached 520,000 in 1790, and of those 425,000 were slaves. [...] while its sugar represented forty percent of the Atlantic market. [...] with Haitians gaining their independence from France in 1804 [...] After the declaration of independence, no state was willing to trade with Haiti [...] The first American ambassador to Haiti – and with it recognition of Haiti's independence – only came in 1862 [...] Thomas Jefferson, United States President, feared a slave revolt would spread to the United States

gancho: Napoleão mandou cerca de 5.200 soldados poloneses para esmagar a revolução no Haiti. Parte deles mudou de lado, e o novo país deu cidadania aos poloneses. Seus descendentes ainda vivem numa vila haitiana.
explicacao: Em 1802, Napoleão enviou a São Domingos uma meia-brigada polonesa de uns 5.200 homens para reforçar as tropas francesas que tentavam reconquistar a colônia rebelde. Os poloneses talvez esperassem, em troca, a ajuda da França para recuperar a independência da Polônia, repartida entre Prússia, Rússia e Áustria; a alguns, disseram que iam enfrentar uma revolta de presos. Mal chegaram, foram jogados contra os rebeldes negros. Cerca de 4.000 deles morreram, e nas duas tropas, francesa e polonesa, a febre amarela matou mais que as batalhas. Os sobreviventes passaram a admirar os adversários, em quem enxergavam a mesma luta por liberdade que queriam para o próprio país, e uma parte deles acabou passando para o lado dos rebeldes (quantos, os historiadores divergem). Depois da independência, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, o primeiro governante do Haiti, poupou os poloneses do massacre que ordenou contra a maior parte dos brancos franceses. Deu-lhes cidadania plena e os classificou como "negros", a categoria que formava a nova classe dominante, e chegou a chamá-los de "os negros brancos da Europa". Calcula-se que 400 a 500 se fixaram no país. A vila de Cazale, a uns 30 km de Porto Príncipe, é o principal núcleo dos descendentes, muitos deles identificáveis por olhos claros e cabelos mais lisos.

fontes.trecho: Cazale, a small village in the hills about 30 kilometres (19 mi) away from Port-au-Prince, is considered the main center of population of the ethnic Polish community in Haiti [...] Some 400 to 500 of these Poles are believed to have settled in Haiti after the war. [...] In May 1802, Napoleon dispatched the 3rd Polish Half-Brigade of around 5,200 men to join French forces in Saint-Domingue [...] The Poles may have been hoping to receive French support in restoring Poland's independence from its occupiers—Prussia (later Germany), Russia, and Austria [...] Some were told that there was a revolt of prisoners in Saint-Domingue. [...] they were quickly thrown into battle against Black rebels. Both French and Polish soldiers in the colony experienced high mortality rates, with more troops dying of yellow fever than from being killed in action. Approximately 4,000 of the 5,200 Polish soldiers sent to Saint-Domingue died. Surviving Polish soldiers admired their opponents, and some 500 or so of them would eventually turn on the French army and joined the rebels. [...] many would come to believe that the former slaves were fighting for the same ideals of freedom and independence to which they, the Poles, aspired. [...] After Haiti gained its independence, Dessalines recognized the Poles and spared them when he ordered the massacre of the establishment of slavery, which consisted of most French whites [...] He granted the Poles classification as Noir (black), who constituted the new ruling class, and in the constitution granted them full Haitian citizenship. [...] Haiti's first head of state Jean-Jacques Dessalines would join Boisrond-Tonnerre in calling the Polish people "the White Negroes of Europe" [...] To this day, Polish Haitians are mixed race and often identified by such European features as blonde or lighter and straighter hair, light eyes
It is the main population center of the Polish community in Haiti, called La Pologne (Poland). [...] The village is populated by descendants of Polish soldiers sent by Napoleon in 1802.

gancho: O 8 de março é o Dia da Mulher por causa de uma revolução: nesse dia, em 1917, operárias têxteis de Petrogrado iniciaram os protestos que derrubaram o czar. A greve de Nova York em 1857 é mito.
explicacao: A ideia de um dia das mulheres nasceu entre socialistas. O primeiro "Dia da Mulher" foi feito em Nova York em 1909, e, em 1910, uma conferência em Copenhague aprovou uma data anual, mas sem dia fixo. Na Rússia de 1917, que ainda usava o calendário juliano, a data caiu em 23 de fevereiro, que no calendário gregoriano era 8 de março. Naquele dia, operárias têxteis de Petrogrado saíram em protesto por "pão e paz", contra a guerra, a falta de comida e o czarismo, e o movimento tomou a cidade inteira. Começava a Revolução de Fevereiro. Sete dias depois, o czar Nicolau II abdicou, e o governo provisório deu às mulheres o direito de voto. Trótski escreveu depois que os revolucionários não imaginavam que aquele Dia da Mulher fosse inaugurar a revolução: as operárias largaram o trabalho contra as ordens e pediram apoio à greve. Em 1921, numa conferência internacional de mulheres comunistas, uma delegada russa propôs fixar a data em 8 de março, em memória das manifestações de Petrogrado, e a proposta passou por unanimidade. A data se espalhou pelos países comunistas e, em 1977, passou a ser promovida pela ONU. Já a versão de que ela lembra um protesto de costureiras em Nova York em 8 de março de 1857 é descrita por pesquisadores como mito.

fontes.trecho: The holiday was promoted by the United Nations in 1977. [...] The earliest reported Women's Day event, called "Woman's Day", was held on 28 February 1909, in New York City. [...] There have been claims that the day was commemorating a protest by women garment workers in New York on 8 March 1857, but researchers have described this as a myth. [...] proposed the establishment of an annual "Women's Day", although no date was specified. [...] On 8 March 1917, in Petrograd (23 February in the Julian calendar), women textile workers began a demonstration that eventually engulfed the whole city, demanding "Bread and Peace"—an end to World War I, to food shortages, and to Tsarism. This marked the beginning of the February Revolution [...] But we did not imagine that this 'Women's Day' would inaugurate the revolution. Revolutionary actions were foreseen but without a date. But in the morning, despite the orders to the contrary, textile workers left their work in several factories and sent delegates to ask for the support of the strike [...] Seven days later, Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, and the provisional Government granted women the right to vote. [...] the third world congress of Communist International in 1921 [...] The date of International Women's Day was also first fixed as March 8 at this Second International Conference of Communist Women. [...] Nikolaeva, a representative of the RSFSR, proposed to set the current date (March 8) in memory of the participation of Petrograd women in the demonstrations of March 8, 1917 that led to the overthrow of the monarchy, which was approved unanimously. After its adoption in Soviet Russia, International Women's Day was predominantly celebrated in communist countries [...] In August 1910, an International Socialist Women's Conference was organized ahead of the general meeting of the Socialist Second International in Copenhagen, Denmark.

gancho: As cenas clássicas da tomada do Palácio de Inverno, em 1917, com combates ferozes, vêm de uma encenação de 1920 e do filme de Eisenstein. Na vida real, o palácio caiu quase sem resistência.
explicacao: Na noite de 25 de outubro de 1917 pelo calendário então usado na Rússia, multidões de insurgentes cercaram o Palácio de Inverno, em Petrogrado, sede do Governo Provisório, e muitos já se infiltravam no prédio. Às 9 e 45 da noite, o cruzador Aurora disparou um tiro de festim. Os primeiros revolucionários entraram às 10 e 25, a entrada em massa veio três horas depois, e às 2 e 10 da madrugada os bolcheviques controlavam o palácio. Os cadetes e as 140 voluntárias do Batalhão Feminino se renderam sem resistir. Mais tarde, historiadores e autoridades soviéticas passaram a contar o episódio em tom heroico. Em 1920, uma grande encenação chamada "A Tomada do Palácio de Inverno" foi assistida por 100 mil pessoas e virou modelo para os filmes oficiais. O mais famoso, "Outubro", de Serguei Eisenstein, lançado em 1928, se inspirou mais nessa encenação do que no evento real, bem menos fotogênico. Como não havia filmagens nem fotos do episódio de verdade, as cenas de Eisenstein acabaram usadas por historiadores e cineastas como se fossem o registro histórico. Segundo as memórias de Alexander Gorodnitsky, que reproduz um relato do pai, o filme quase não tinha atores profissionais: Lênin foi interpretado por um operário de uma fábrica de cimento.

fontes.trecho: It began through an insurrection in Petrograd (now Saint Petersburg) on 7 November 1917 [O.S. 25 October]. [...] As the night progressed, crowds of insurgents surrounded the palace, and many infiltrated it. At 9:45 p.m, the cruiser Aurora fired a blank shot from the harbor. Some of the revolutionaries entered the palace at 10:25 p.m. and there was a mass entry 3 hours later. By 2:10 a.m. on 26 October, Bolshevik forces had gained control. The cadets and the 140 volunteers of the Women's Battalion surrendered rather than resist [...] While the seizure of the Winter Palace happened almost without resistance, Soviet historians and officials later tended to depict the event in dramatic and heroic terms. The historical reenactment titled The Storming of the Winter Palace was staged in 1920. This reenactment, watched by 100,000 spectators, provided the model for official films made later, which showed fierce fighting during the storming of the Winter Palace, although, in reality, the Bolshevik insurgents had faced little opposition.

fontes.titulo: October: Ten Days That Shook the World
fontes.trecho: The scene of the storming was based more on The Storming of the Winter Palace (1920) [...] than the original occasion, which was far less photogenic. This scene became the legitimate, historical depiction of the storming of the Winter Palace owing to the lack of print or film documenting the actual event, which led historians and filmmakers to use Eisenstein's recreation. [...] According to the memoirs of Alexander Gorodnitsky, his father Moisei described that "in the film October there were almost no professional actors. Lenin, for example was played by Nikandrov, a cement factory worker [...] 1928

gancho: A revolução que derrubou o último imperador da China foi precipitada por um acidente: uma bomba explodiu sem querer na oficina dos rebeldes. E Sun Yat-sen, o futuro presidente, estava nos EUA e soube pelo jornal.
explicacao: Em 1911, dois grupos revolucionários de Wuhan preparavam um levante contra a dinastia Qing. Ele foi marcado para 6 de outubro, na Festa do Meio do Outono, e depois adiado por falta de preparo. Em 9 de outubro, enquanto o revolucionário Sun Wu supervisionava a fabricação de explosivos na concessão russa de Hankou, um dos artefatos explodiu e o feriu gravemente. No hospital, descobriram quem ele era e avisaram as autoridades. Com a identidade dos conspiradores revelada e a prisão iminente, os rebeldes infiltrados no Novo Exército decidiram agir na hora. Na noite de 10 de outubro, eles se amotinaram em Wuchang e tomaram a residência do vice-rei. O levante se espalhou, e até o fim de dezembro 18 províncias do sul e do centro tinham rompido com o governo Qing. Sun Yat-sen, que não deve ser confundido com Sun Wu, estava nos Estados Unidos pedindo dinheiro a chineses emigrados. Recebeu um telegrama de um companheiro, mas não conseguiu decifrá-lo, e soube do levante pelos jornais. Voltou à China, foi eleito presidente provisório e, em 1º de janeiro de 1912, foi fundada a República da China. Em 12 de fevereiro de 1912, o trono Qing abdicou em nome do imperador Puyi, encerrando mais de 2.000 anos de governo imperial.

fontes.trecho: These groups, led by Jiang Yiwu and Sun Wu respectively, worked closely together [...] Beginning in September 1911, these two groups began negotiating with the Tongmenghui [...] The date was originally set for 6 October, on the Mid-Autumn festival. The date was later postponed, due to inadequate preparations. On 9 October, while Sun Wu was supervising the making of explosive devices in the Russian concession in Hankou, one of the devices exploded unexpectedly, inflicting serious injuries on Sun. When he was hospitalized, the hospital staff discovered his identity and alerted the Qing authorities. [...] With their identities revealed, the revolutionaries in the New Army stationed in Wuchang were facing imminent arrest by the Qing authorities. The decision was made by Jiang Yiwu of the Wenxueshe to immediately launch the uprising [...] On the evening of 10 October, Wu Zhaolin as provisional commander led the revolutionary elements of the New Army and staged a mutiny against the Qing garrison in Huguang, capturing the residence of the Viceroy [...] Sun Yat-sen was traveling in the United States speaking to overseas Chinese to appeal for financial support when the uprising took place. Although Sun received a telegram from Huang Xing, he was unable to decipher it, and found out about the uprising the next morning in the newspaper. [...] eighteen provinces in Southern and Central China agreed to secede from the Qing government by the end of December 1911. [...] Sun returned to China to participate in the provisional presidential election and was elected. Representatives from the seceding provinces met on 1 January 1912, and declared the founding of the Republic of China [...] On 12 February 1912, Empress Dowager Longyu, on behalf of Puyi, the Xuantong Emperor, announced the abdication of the Qing throne, marking the end of the dynasty.
to overthrow the last emperor, Puyi. That put Huang in charge of the revolution that ended over 2000 years of imperial rule in China.

gancho: A senha para começar a revolução que derrubou a ditadura em Portugal, em 1974, foi tocar no rádio a canção do país no Festival Eurovisão. E os primeiros cravos vieram de um restaurante que festejava um ano de vida.
explicacao: Os militares que planejavam derrubar o Estado Novo combinaram dois sinais secretos pelo rádio. Às 22h55 de 24 de abril de 1974, um locutor anunciou a hora e tocou "E Depois do Adeus", de Paulo de Carvalho, que representara Portugal no Eurovisão daquele ano: era o aviso para os capitães começarem. Às 0h20 do dia 25, a Rádio Renascença tocou "Grândola, Vila Morena", de Zeca Afonso, cantor com muitas músicas proibidas nas rádios, e as tropas partiram para tomar os pontos estratégicos. As letras eram inofensivas, porque a censura não deixaria passar nada mais inflamado; o recado estava no simples fato de tocá-las. De manhã, em Lisboa, a faxineira Celeste Caeiro chegou ao restaurante onde trabalhava, que completava um ano e ia distribuir cravos aos clientes.
